title: Ecclesiastes 5:1–7
context: Ecclesiastes 5:1–7 turns to approaching God: listen rather than offer the sacrifice of fools, speak few words before God, pay vows promptly, and above all fear God. The passage connects with the book’s wider teaching that all things have their time under God (3:1–8, 3:14). In Hebrew Bibles, English 5:1 is numbered 4:17 and 5:2–20 is numbered 5:1–19; the WEB verse numbers are kept here. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about reverent, sincere worship.

verses.text: Guard your steps when you go to God’s house; for to draw near to listen is better than to give the sacrifice of fools, for they don’t know that they do evil.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Preacher urges care in approaching God’s house: drawing near to listen is better than offering the sacrifice of fools. Attentive worship matters more than ritual alone.

Arminian readers see a call to sincere, responsive hearing.
verses.reformedNotes:
The saying resembles other biblical warnings that obedience and listening outweigh sacrifice (compare 1 Samuel 15:22).

Reformed readers see worship ruled by God’s word rather than human display. Both traditions read this as shared ground about reverent, attentive worship.

verses.text: Don’t be rash with your mouth, and don’t let your heart be hasty to utter anything before God; for God is in heaven, and you on earth. Therefore let your words be few.
verses.arminianNotes:
Do not be rash with your mouth or hasty to speak before God, for God is in heaven and you are on earth, so let your words be few. Reverence shapes speech.

Arminian readers see humility before God in prayer and promise.
verses.reformedNotes:
The contrast between heaven and earth grounds the call to restraint. It does not forbid prayer but warns against careless words.

Reformed readers see the Creator–creature distinction honored in worship. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground.

verses.text: For as a dream comes with a multitude of cares, so a fool’s speech with a multitude of words.
verses.arminianNotes:
As dreams come with many cares, so a fool’s speech comes with many words. Excess marks both.

Arminian readers see a practical warning that a flood of words often reveals a lack of thought rather than depth of devotion.
verses.reformedNotes:
The proverb links restless activity and restless talk. Its exact sense is compact, but the point about many words is clear.

Reformed readers see wisdom in measured speech before God. Both traditions read this as shared ground about guarding the tongue.

verses.text: When you vow a vow to God, don’t defer to pay it; for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay that which you vow.
verses.arminianNotes:
When you make a vow to God, do not delay in paying it, for he has no pleasure in fools; pay what you vow. Promises to God are serious.

Arminian readers see real accountability for freely made commitments.
verses.reformedNotes:
The teaching echoes Deuteronomy 23:21–23, which also warns against delaying a vow and says refraining from vowing is no sin.

Reformed readers see God’s holiness requiring faithfulness in speech. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: It is better that you should not vow, than that you should vow and not pay.
verses.arminianNotes:
It is better not to vow than to vow and not pay. Restraint is wiser than empty promises.

Arminian readers see freedom not to vow paired with a duty to keep any vow that is made, so that words before God remain truthful.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse does not discourage devotion but warns against careless or impulsive commitments.

Reformed readers see integrity required of worshipers. Both traditions read this as shared ground about honesty before God and the weight of words spoken in his presence.

verses.text: Don’t allow your mouth to lead you into sin. Don’t protest before the messenger that this was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice, and destroy the work of your hands?
verses.arminianNotes:
Do not let your mouth lead you into sin or tell the messenger it was a mistake, lest God be angry and destroy the work of your hands. Excuses do not undo careless vows.

Arminian readers see responsibility for one’s words.
verses.reformedNotes:
The identity of ‘the messenger’ is debated; proposals include a priest or temple official, or an angel, and the text does not specify.

Reformed readers see God taking vows seriously. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: For in the multitude of dreams there are vanities, as well as in many words; but you must fear God.
verses.arminianNotes:
Many dreams and many words bring vanity, but you must fear God. The section closes with its central command.

Arminian readers see the fear of God as a reverent, freely chosen orientation of life that guards worship from empty talk.
verses.reformedNotes:
The command to fear God recurs in the book and reaches its fullest statement at 12:13.

Reformed readers see the fear of God as the root of true worship. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground and see it as the heart of 5:1–7.
